tldr: Salm walks through Spring AI's core building blocks (ChatModel and ChatClient, structured output, the Advisor API, RAG, @Tool and MCP) as the harness that compensates for what LLMs cannot do alone.
summary: Salm, a solution architect at Broadcom, frames Spring AI as a harness around the model: LLMs predict tokens without verifying facts, are stateless, only know their public training data and cannot act. The usual remedies (memory, RAG, tool calling) raise new problems in turn: token cost, context limits, an attack surface when the model decides which tool to call, and the need for governance and observability. Spring AI builds on Spring Boot auto-configuration, so switching provider (OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, Anthropic, Ollama) is mostly a dependency and configuration change; Spring AI 2.0 requires Spring Boot 4. Using a recipe-finder sample, he shows the low-level ChatModel and ImageModel APIs with PromptTemplate, then the fluent ChatClient built from an auto-configured ChatClient.Builder with a default system prompt, and .entity() for structured output, which works natively or by adding a JSON schema to the prompt.

The Advisor API, which works like REST client interceptors and supports both blocking and streaming calls, is the basis of the advanced features. Advisors run as an ordered chain, so a logging advisor should sit after RAG to see the full prompt. For RAG he shows indexing with document readers, splitters and VectorStore.add, then retrieval with QuestionAnswerAdvisor using a SearchRequest with topK and a similarity threshold, plus a more modular RAG implementation. Recursive advisors copy the chain to run sub-loops such as LLM-based evaluation or structured-output validation with retry. Tools are plain methods annotated with @Tool and @ToolParam and passed via .tools(). MCP clients only need a server URL in configuration; servers use the MCP server starter and @McpTool. Observability through OpenTelemetry and testing with LLM evaluators were mentioned only briefly; a free Spring Academy course covers the rest.
keyPoints: Spring AI 2.0 requires Spring Boot 4; provider switching is done through starters and configuration, not code changes.

ChatClient (fluent, built from an injected ChatClient.Builder) is the main API; .entity(Recipe.class) returns structured output, falling back to schema instructions in the prompt when the provider has no native support.
Advisors are an ordered interceptor chain around model calls; RAG, memory, validation and logging are all implemented as advisors.
QuestionAnswerAdvisor gives basic RAG with a configurable topK and similarity threshold; recursive advisors enable evaluation and retry loops.
@Tool and @ToolParam expose Java methods to the model; @McpTool exposes them to other agents over MCP.
takeaways: Learn ChatClient and the Advisor API first; most other Spring AI features are built on them.
Use .entity() structured output to slot LLM calls into ordinary typed Java workflows.
Place logging advisors after RAG and other context-adding advisors so you see the prompt that actually reaches the model.
Keep the tool set small and run agents in restricted environments, since the model decides which tools to call.
watchIf: You are a Spring developer who has not used Spring AI yet and want a compact tour of its core APIs before building RAG or agentic features.
